correctness.rationale: For k>=3 the defining piecewise-linear decreasing sum has a unique root h; its half-residual coefficients p_i form a probability distribution. Every stable-set vertex has squared distance B+s(1-2p_i), and a_i(1-2p_i)=min(a_i,h), which proves ball containment and the exact contact classification. The center is a convex combination of only equality contacts, so the weighted variance identity forces every competing center y to have squared enclosing radius at least R^2+||y-c||^2, proving global optimality and uniqueness. Solving the active-set sum yields h=(m-2)/H and the claimed rational radius. Adding classes no larger than h leaves the root and center unchanged. All parameters and equality boundaries are explicit.

originality.rationale: The same-object framework and perfect-graph stable-set facet/vertex literature were examined in open-access primary full text. Neither inspected source contains a Euclidean circumradius, minimum enclosing center, or full-class screening theorem. Published-result searches included stable-set polytope, perfect graph, complete multipartite, anchored coordinate cubes, free sum of cubes, Chebyshev center, and minimum enclosing sphere aliases. No theorem implying the exact rational large-part screening law was identified; the closest previous metric finding for perfect stable-set polytopes addresses the INSCRIBED radius, which does not imply the outer-radius result.
residual_risks: The same convex body is a hull of disjointly supported anchored coordinate cubes, and an equivalent geometric calculation may exist without graph terminology.
General convex-hull minimum-ball algorithms can in principle solve finite instances but do not immediately provide the exact active-class threshold or invariance principle.
The weighted contact identity is elementary once the full-class support is recognized, so rediscovery is plausible.
Search nonappearance is not a global proof of novelty or independent certification.

value.rationale: The unsymmetrized stable-set polytope is a basic object in perfect-graph and 2-level convex geometry. Determining its exact Euclidean outer sphere across all complete multipartite part-size profiles is a natural metric complement to facet and counting results. The theorem does more than compute a radius: it gives unique centers, a complete supporting contact classification, rational piecewise-harmonic formulas and a stable screening threshold that permits arbitrarily many extra graph vertices/classes without changing the radius. These are genuine structure and extremal invariance results, rather than arbitrary small-parameter enumeration.
